hints: Start by writing out what actually happens when ammonia meets water, and watch where the hydrogen ion goes.
Remember ammonia changes from pyramidal with a lone pair to tetrahedral when it gains an extra $\text{H}^+$, so think about how shape and angle change.
Check oxidation numbers and proton transfer to decide if this is redox or simply an acid-base proton donation.
walkthrough:
**Write the reaction**

Think of this as ammonia borrowing a proton from water. It is a classic Bronsted-Lowry acid-base reaction.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{NH}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons \text{NH}_4^+ + \text{OH}^-$$

**Identify acid and base**

An acid donates an $\text{H}^+$ and a base accepts it. Here water gives an $\text{H}^+$ to ammonia, so water is the acid and ammonia is the base.

**Check shape, polarity and oxidation state**

$\text{NH}_3$ is trigonal pyramidal with a lone pair, bond angle about $107^{\circ}$, and it is polar so it has a dipole moment. $\text{NH}_4^+$ is perfectly tetrahedral, bond angle $109.5^{\circ}$, and symmetrical so it has no net dipole. Oxidation numbers stay the same ($\text{N}$ is -3, $\text{H}$ is +1, $\text{O}$ is -2), so this is not redox.

options.A: Incorrect. Ammonia, $\text{NH}_3$, is pyramidal and unsymmetrical with a lone pair, so the bond dipoles do not cancel and it does have a permanent dipole moment. Only the symmetrical tetrahedral $\text{NH}_4^+$ has no net dipole.
options.B: Incorrect. The angles are the wrong way round. Ammonia has 3 bonds plus 1 lone pair which squeezes the angle to about $107^{\circ}$, while ammonium has 4 equal bonds and no lone pair, giving the perfect tetrahedral angle of $109.5^{\circ}$.
options.C: Incorrect. No electrons are transferred. Nitrogen stays at -3, hydrogen at +1 and oxygen at -2 on both sides. This is proton transfer, not oxidation and reduction.
options.D: Correct. Water donates a proton ($\text{H}^+$) to ammonia to form $\text{NH}_4^+$ and $\text{OH}^-$. By the Bronsted-Lowry definition, a proton donor is an acid, so water is acting as the acid here.
